results.question: What is the half-life of carbon-14 used in radiocarbon dating?
points: 说明它用于放射性碳定年

official.finalText:
The half-life of carbon-14 (¹⁴C) used in radiocarbon dating is about **5,700 years** — commonly given as **5,730 ± 40 years** (the "Cambridge" value) [1][2], with the older "Libby" value of **5,568 years** still sometimes cited [3].

Note that radiocarbon ages are conventionally reported in "radiocarbon years" using the Libby half-life and then calibrated to calendar years, so the precise half-life matters mainly for the calibration and for the method's usable range (~50,000 years) [4].

Sources:
- [Radiocarbon dating — Nature Reviews Methods Primers](https://experiments.springernature.com/nature/primers/10.1038/s43586-021-00058-7)
- [Education — Stable Isotopes, NOAA GML](https://gmd-int.cmdl.noaa.gov/infodata/isotopes/decay.html)
- [Radiocarbon Dating — H. P. Schwarcz](https://www.taylorfrancis.com/chapters/edit/10.4324/9781315663999-12/radiocarbon-dating-schwarcz)
- [The Half-Life of ¹⁴C — Why Is It So Long? (Radiocarbon, Cambridge Core)](http://core-prod.cambridgecore.org/core/journals/radiocarbon/article/abs/halflife-of-14cwhy-is-it-so-long/40C969D635697E923338763B56402862)
